title: Disease detectives: follow the cause
subtitle: Sort the evidence, trace transmission and avoid a false conclusion
objective: Distinguish communicable and non-communicable disease using cause and transmission evidence.

sow.alignment: Directly develops the Week 6 outcome using Pearson 5.2 and 5.4–5.6. This exemplar selects representative infections; it does not replace all Topic 5 disease examples.

priorLearning: A microorganism is microscopic; not all microorganisms cause disease.
A cause differs from an observed symptom.
success: Classify a disease from its cause and transmission route.
Explain an indirect transmission route and how an intervention could interrupt it.
Explain why a shared symptom or risk factor is not proof of a diagnosis.

vocabulary.meaning: A disease whose infectious cause can spread between organisms, directly or indirectly.
A disease that is not transmitted between organisms.
A disease-causing agent, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.
An organism that carries a pathogen between hosts.
Something associated with a higher chance of a disease; it does not guarantee it.
A change experienced by a person that may be associated with illness.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one selected response route; pen, ruler and calculator.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint. Optional word processor or spreadsheet.
preparation: Print the shared evidence page, one chosen response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the teacher answers before teaching. All numerical sample data in this lesson are constructed for learning.
safety: Paper and screen tasks; no biological sampling, cultures, medicine handling or personal health disclosures.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is included. Point, annotate, dictate or discuss quietly instead of writing or using a device.

misconceptions.claim: All disease spreads by touching someone.
misconceptions.correction: Some infectious causes spread through air, water or vectors; non-communicable diseases are not transmitted.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to trace the malaria card without a direct person-to-person arrow.

misconceptions.claim: Two people coughing must have the same infection.
misconceptions.correction: Different causes can produce a similar symptom; symptoms alone cannot establish a cause.

misconceptions.claim: A risk factor makes a disease certain.
misconceptions.correction: Risk factors alter probability and may interact; they do not guarantee an outcome.
misconceptions.check: Replace “will” with a justified risk statement.

misconceptions.correction: Antibiotics target bacterial processes; they do not treat viruses.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether the influenza card supplies a bacterial target.

access.supported: Same core scientific goal, with word bank, short prompts, read-aloud or pointing/dictation. Do not assign a route from diagnosis.
access.standard: Use the supplied evidence to explain and justify an independent scientific decision.
access.stretch: Optional challenge after secure core: evaluate a limitation and transfer the science. Higher-tier-only material, where present, is labelled explicitly.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer solo or partner work, a pass and quiet response. Allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task; no compulsory disclosure, performance or speed competition.

slides.title: One symptom. Two explanations.
body: Mission: solve disease evidence cards without guessing a diagnosis.
You may point, discuss quietly or write.
slides.notes: Ask whether a cough proves an infection. Hold the question open until the two cause cards are compared. We classify supplied examples; we do not classify classmates.

slides.title: Cause, symptom or risk?
body: R1. Are all microorganisms harmful?
R2. Is a symptom the same as its cause?
R3. Does a higher chance mean certainty?
slides.notes: R1 no; many microorganisms are harmless or useful. R2 no; the same symptom may have different causes. R3 no. If unsure, use an everyday chance example without asking for health stories.

slides.title: I follow the causal evidence
body: My first question: is there a transmissible infectious cause?
I do not classify from how unwell someone looks.
slides.notes: Model: “A says bacteria can spread through air, so I classify tuberculosis as communicable. D says asthma is not transmitted. Both can involve coughing, so cough alone cannot decide.”

visual.title: Classify using the cause, not the symptom
visual.description: A branching comparison: communicable disease involves a transmissible infectious cause; non-communicable disease is not transmitted. Cough is deliberately shown with both tuberculosis and asthma.

elements.text: Classify using the cause, not the symptom

Asthma: airway condition
Cough can occur
The same symptom can have different causes.

slides.title: Transmission can be indirect
body: A vector can carry a pathogen between hosts.
Follow the arrows and name the pathogen.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “The protist causes malaria. The mosquito carries it. Therefore I need not draw a direct touch between people. I must not call the mosquito the pathogen.” The simplified route omits the parasite life cycle and does not predict whether an individual bite infects.

visual.title: Malaria: a vector connects hosts
visual.description: A simplified malaria transmission model. An infected person may infect a mosquito feeding on them; an infected mosquito can pass the malaria protist to another person when biting. Not every mosquito is a malaria vector; this is a route model, not a forecast.

elements.text:
Pathogen may enter
mosquito during feed

A route through a vector is still communicable.
A bite does not automatically mean infection.

slides.title: A careful explanation of risk
body: Several factors can affect disease risk.
“More likely” is different from “will happen”.
slides.notes: Model: “The heart-disease card gives several influences. It cannot tell me whether a named person will develop disease. A claim blaming one behaviour ignores genes, environment and access to resources.” No personal disclosures.

visual.title: Risk is not a single switch
visual.description: A conceptual risk diagram with inherited, environmental and behavioural factors converging on the probability of a non-communicable disease. No numerical prediction or blame is implied.

elements.text: Risk is not a single switch

Can alter the chance
of disease
Risk is not certainty. Illness is not a blame label.

slides.title: Case-board challenge
body: W1. Sort A–F into communicable or non-communicable.
Use the cause column as evidence.
slides.notes: Give silent think time. Invite one choice plus reason, then ask another pupil to test the reason with a counterexample. A/B/C/F communicable; D/E non-communicable. Use printable cards or interactive reveal, same science.

table.caption: Supplied teaching summaries; not diagnostic guidance.

slides.title: Interrupt one route
body: W2. Choose a route: cholera or malaria.
Match it to safer water/food or a mosquito barrier.
Explain the link rather than naming a cure.
slides.notes: Cholera: safer water/food reduces exposure to water/food-borne bacteria. Malaria: mosquito barriers such as insecticide-treated nets can reduce vector bites, depending on use/context. These are mechanism examples, not travel advice. Ask what part of the route is interrupted.

visual.title: Malaria: a vector connects hosts
visual.description: A simplified malaria transmission model. An infected person may infect a mosquito feeding on them; an infected mosquito can pass the malaria protist to another person when biting. Not every mosquito is a malaria vector; this is a route model, not a forecast.

elements.text:
Pathogen may enter
mosquito during feed

A route through a vector is still communicable.
A bite does not automatically mean infection.

slides.title: Repair the false headline
body: W3. “Both people cough, so both have the same communicable disease.”
Use A and D to improve the headline.
slides.notes: Expected: cough can have different causes; tuberculosis is communicable, asthma is not. Evidence about cause is needed. Ask the audience to say which exact word was too strong. No actual diagnosis is attempted.
slides.reveal: The same symptom can have different causes. These two cause cards belong in different categories.

slides.title: Which statement is scientifically sound?
body: Choose, then justify with a card.
slides.notes: Correct B. If pupils select A, return to vector diagram; if C, compare cause and symptom; if D, revisit risk diagram.

options.text: Malaria is non-communicable because a vector is involved.
options.feedback: A pathogen can spread indirectly through a vector; malaria is communicable.

options.text: A communicable disease has an infectious cause that can spread.
options.feedback: Yes. Spread can be direct or indirect, including air, water and vectors.

options.text: A shared symptom proves the same cause.
options.feedback: Tuberculosis and asthma can both involve coughing but have different causes.
A risk factor affects probability; it does not make disease certain.

slides.title: Build an evidence-based explanation
body: Choose your agreed response page.
Use the supplied cards, not personal health examples.
slides.notes: Set one route. Pupils produce a case classification, a transmission explanation and a cautious conclusion. Route selection responds to current support needs.

slides.title: Independent case report
body: Classify → cite a clue → trace a route → check a claim.
Aim for accurate reasoning, not a long answer.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Circulate after first classification. For wrong malaria category, trace person–vector–person without revealing the category. For blame statements, redirect to multiple factors.

slides.title: Let evidence change a decision
body: L1. Offer one classification and your strongest clue.
Your audience asks: “Does that clue identify the cause?”
slides.notes: A partner, teacher or TA is an audience; quiet written review is valid. Ask a genuine challenge; pupil improves or defends using source evidence. Do not publicly rank health knowledge.

slides.title: A defensible case report
body: Name the category and causal evidence.
Keep probability separate from certainty.
slides.notes: Share model: “C is communicable: a mosquito can carry the malaria protist between hosts. The mosquito is the vector, not the pathogen.” Ask pupils to amend one term if needed.

slides.title: Three scientific distinctions
body: E1. Define communicable.
E2. Name malaria’s pathogen type and vector.
E3. Why can cough alone not classify a disease?
slides.notes: E1 transmissible infectious cause. E2 protist; mosquito. E3 different causes can cause a similar symptom. Use responses to plan barrier/immune lesson.

slides.title: Your next useful step
body: Circle one: cause • route • risk.
Keep one explanation you improved.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Collect one response per pupil, accepting annotated arrows or dictated words. If cause remains insecure, begin next lesson with A versus D.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Disease case board
pupilPages.intro: Teaching summaries for classification. Do not use these cards to diagnose yourself or anyone else.

cards.title: A | Tuberculosis
cards.text: Caused by bacteria. The infectious cause can pass through the air. Coughing can occur.

cards.title: B | Cholera
cards.text: Caused by bacteria. People can become infected through contaminated water or food.

cards.title: C | Malaria
cards.text: Caused by protists. Certain mosquitoes can carry the pathogen between people.

cards.title: D | Asthma
cards.text: A non-communicable airway condition. Coughing can occur; asthma is not passed between people.

cards.title: E | Coronary heart disease
cards.text: A non-communicable disease. Inherited, environmental and behavioural factors can affect risk.

cards.title: F | Influenza
cards.text: Caused by influenza viruses. Infection can spread between people; antibiotics do not treat the virus.

blocks.prompt: W1. Sort A–F. W2. Explain a route interruption. W3. Repair the cough headline.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Follow the evidence
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: communicable; non-communicable; pathogen; bacteria; protist; vector; not certain.

blocks.prompt: S1. Put A–F into the two disease categories. Give one clue for C and one for D.
S2. Complete the malaria route using person, mosquito and protist. What is the vector?
S3. Choose safer water/food or a mosquito barrier for cholera. Explain which route it interrupts.
S4. Why does a shared cough not prove the same cause? Use A and D.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Write the case report
pupilPages.intro: Use the shared cards. Short, precise scientific sentences are enough.

blocks.prompt: M1. Classify A–F and justify two different communicable transmission routes.
M2. Explain how a malaria barrier could reduce transmission. Distinguish pathogen and vector.
M3. Explain why coughing alone cannot show whether a disease is communicable.
M4. Improve: “A risk factor means someone will develop heart disease.” Include more than one type of influence.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Challenge the conclusion
pupilPages.intro: Optional transfer. New fictional cases: G is caused by a fungus whose spores pass through air. H is an inherited blood condition with no infectious cause.

blocks.prompt: T1. Classify G and H. Explain why “inherited” is not the same as communicable.
T2. A town reports more coughing after dusty construction work. Does this prove an infectious outbreak? Give another plausible cause and one type of additional evidence.
T3. A poster says antibiotics cure every communicable disease. Evaluate it using two pathogen types from the cards.
T4. Explain why a prevention method can reduce risk without guaranteeing that no infection occurs.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Cause, route, risk
pupilPages.intro: Use accurate scientific words or annotated arrows.

blocks.prompt: E1. What makes a disease communicable?
E2. Name malaria’s pathogen type and its vector.
E3. Why is cough alone insufficient to classify a disease?
L1. What did your audience ask? Which explanation did you improve or defend?

answers.label: Retrieval R1–R3
answers.answer: R1 no. R2 a symptom is not its cause; different causes may produce a similar symptom. R3 increased chance is not certainty.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 A/B/C/F communicable; D/E non-communicable. W2 safer water/food interrupts the cholera ingestion route; a suitable mosquito barrier reduces malaria-vector bites. W3 cough alone cannot establish cause: A and D provide a counterexample.

answers.label: Hinge A–D
answers.answer: A false: indirect vector spread is communicable. B correct: a transmissible infectious cause defines the category. C false: shared symptoms do not prove shared cause. D false: a risk factor does not guarantee disease.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: A/B/C/F communicable; D/E non-communicable. C: protist carried by mosquito. D: airway condition not transmitted. Examples of different routes: airborne tuberculosis versus contaminated water/food in cholera.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: An infected person can infect a feeding mosquito; an infected mosquito can pass the protist to another person through a bite. Protist = pathogen; mosquito = vector. A barrier reduces opportunities for infectious bites; it does not treat infection.

answers.label: S3
answers.answer: Safer water/food reduces exposure to cholera bacteria entering through contaminated water/food. A mosquito barrier does not target this transmission route.

answers.label: S4 / M3
answers.answer: A and D can both involve coughing but have different causes/categories. Cough alone cannot establish the infectious cause or diagnose either condition.

answers.label: M4
answers.answer: A risk factor can increase the chance of disease, not guarantee it. Genetic/body factors, environment and behaviour/circumstances can combine. Do not accept blame or certainty as an explanation.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: G communicable: fungal spores carry the infectious cause through air. H non-communicable: an inherited condition is passed through genetic information at reproduction, not transmitted as an infection.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: No. Dust exposure can cause irritation or trigger airway symptoms. Additional evidence could include appropriate clinical/pathogen testing or exposure histories; pupils do not perform these tests. A temporal association alone cannot establish the cause.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: False: antibiotics may be used against some bacterial infections; they do not treat influenza viruses. Classification as communicable alone does not determine a treatment. Clinical decisions are outside this task.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Barriers may not remove every exposure and effectiveness depends on use/context; reducing the chance of transmission does not make it impossible.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 a disease whose infectious cause can spread directly or indirectly. E2 malaria protist; mosquito vector. E3 similar symptoms can have different causes.

answers.label: L1 and assessment
answers.answer: Accept any specific evidence-led revision or justified confirmation. Secure core = correct causal classification, vector/pathogen distinction, and no symptom-to-diagnosis leap. Re-teach with A versus D if a pupil uses cough as the category rule.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 10, We do 7, hinge 3, independent 11, review 3, exit 1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing plus explanation, annotations or writing as evidence.
A quiet review still has an audience: teacher or TA reads the pupil’s decision, asks one evidence question, and the pupil revises or confirms it.
Keep discussion about the fictional or supplied case cards. Pupils need not disclose illnesses, family history or medication.

Interactive We do: predict the case category, test the malaria route, then repair the symptom claim. The paper equivalent is W1–W3 with cards and arrows; the visual is a conceptual route model, not a simulation of infection risk.
